name: Ludwig van Beethoven
bio:
Beethoven grew up in Bonn, in a family of court musicians. His father, a singer, pushed him hard as a child prodigy, and in his teens Ludwig was already playing in the court orchestra and helping to support the family. In 1792 he moved to Vienna to study with Haydn, and he soon made his name there as a ferocious pianist, famous above all for his improvising.

In his late twenties he began to lose his hearing. In 1802, in a letter to his brothers now known as the Heiligenstadt Testament, he admitted that he had thought of ending his life, and that only his art had held him back. What followed was a burst of bold, large-scale works, among them the *Eroica* and the Fifth Symphony. By his last years he was almost completely deaf, yet he kept composing, and wrote the Ninth Symphony and his late string quartets.

Beethoven died in Vienna in 1827, and a huge crowd followed his funeral procession. He changed what people expected music to do: a symphony could now be a personal statement, a struggle that ends in triumph, or a deep meditation. He stretched old forms such as [[sonata-form|sonata form]] until they could hold far more drama than before. Almost every composer who came after him, from Brahms to Mahler, worked in his shadow.

name: Hector Berlioz
bio:
Berlioz was born in 1803 in La Côte-Saint-André, a small town near Grenoble, where his father was a doctor. He was sent to Paris to study medicine, but he hated the dissecting room and spent his evenings at the opera instead. Against his family’s wishes he gave up medicine for music and entered the Paris Conservatoire. Unusually for a composer, he never became a real pianist; his instruments were the flute and the guitar.

In 1827 he saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia and Juliet, and fell obsessively in love with her. That passion poured into the *Symphonie fantastique* of 1830, a piece of [[programme-music|programme music]] about an artist’s love, his opium dreams and a nightmarish witches’ sabbath, with the beloved represented by a returning melody, the [[idee-fixe|idée fixe]]. He did eventually meet and marry Harriet, but the marriage was unhappy.

Berlioz thought in sound and colour, and his book on orchestration was studied by composers for generations. In France he was often misunderstood and made much of his living as a music critic, while audiences in Germany, Russia and England welcomed him as a conductor. His epic opera *Les Troyens* was never staged complete in his lifetime. He died in Paris in 1869.

name: Johannes Brahms
bio:
Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833, the son of a double-bass player who scraped a living in the city’s dance halls and theatres. Johannes was earning money at the piano while still a teenager. In 1853 he met Robert and Clara Schumann, and Robert, then one of the most respected composers in Germany, published an article hailing the twenty-year-old as the future of music.

Schumann’s praise was both a gift and a burden. Brahms worked on his First Symphony for about twenty years, all too aware of Beethoven looking over his shoulder, and it was finally premiered in 1876, when he was 43. After Robert Schumann’s death he remained devoted to Clara for the rest of her life, as friend and confidant; the exact nature of their bond is still debated.

He settled in Vienna in the 1860s and became one of the most admired figures in European music, writing four symphonies, *A German Requiem*, concertos, and a great deal of chamber music and songs. Brahms loved old forms such as the [[variation|variation]] and the [[passacaglia|passacaglia]], and filled them with warm, autumnal feeling. He died in Vienna in 1897, less than a year after Clara.

name: Antonín Dvořák
bio:
Dvořák was born in 1841 in Nelahozeves, a village on the Vltava north of Prague, where his father was a butcher and innkeeper. He was expected to take over the family business, but music won. He studied at the organ school in Prague, then spent years playing the viola in a theatre orchestra, which for a time was conducted by Bedřich Smetana.

Recognition came in his thirties. Brahms sat on the jury that awarded him an Austrian state grant, and he recommended Dvořák to his own publisher, Simrock, who brought out the *Slavonic Dances* in 1878 to huge success. Dvořák’s music, full of the dance rhythms and melodies of Bohemia and Moravia, made him famous across Europe, and especially in England, which he visited nine times.

In 1892 he went to New York as director of the National Conservatory of Music. There he wrote his Ninth Symphony, *From the New World*, and spent a summer among the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa. Homesick, he returned to Bohemia in 1895, later became director of the Prague Conservatory, and wrote his opera *Rusalka*. He died in Prague in 1904.

name: Gustav Mahler
bio:
Mahler was born in 1860 in Kaliště, a village in Bohemia, into a German-speaking Jewish family, and grew up in the nearby town of Jihlava. Many of his parents’ fourteen children died young, and death and loss echo all through his music. As a boy he loved folk songs and the military bands of the local barracks, sounds that later found their way into his symphonies. At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition.

He became one of the greatest conductors of his time. In 1897 he took charge of the Vienna Court Opera, having converted from Judaism to Catholicism shortly before, as the post effectively required. He was a fierce perfectionist, and his demand for fresh, meticulously rehearsed performances won him admirers and enemies in equal measure. For ten demanding years he transformed the company, and he composed in the summers, in small composing huts by lakes and in the mountains.

Mahler is said to have told Sibelius that a symphony must be like the world: it must embrace everything. His symphonies are vast, mixing folk songs, marches, birdsong and moments of deep stillness. After leaving Vienna he conducted in New York, at the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. He died in Vienna in 1911, aged 50, leaving his Tenth Symphony unfinished.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
bio:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the son of Leopold, a violinist and composer who was also a gifted teacher. Wolfgang was writing little pieces by the age of five, and as a child he toured the courts and concert halls of Europe with his father and his older sister, Nannerl, a brilliant keyboard player herself. Those years on the road filled his ears with every musical style of the day, from Italian opera to German counterpoint.

In 1781 he broke with his employer, the Archbishop of Salzburg, and settled in Vienna as a freelance musician, a rare and risky move at the time. He earned his living by teaching, playing his own piano concertos at subscription concerts and selling his music. The Vienna years brought *The Marriage of Figaro*, *Don Giovanni* and *The Magic Flute*, and his last three symphonies, all written within a few weeks in the summer of 1788.

He died in Vienna in December 1791, aged 35, with his *Requiem* unfinished; his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it. What lasts is the feeling that nothing in his music is forced. Melodies that sound effortless turn out to be carefully built, and even the brightest pages can cloud over in a bar or two. That is why his music works on a first hearing and still rewards the hundredth.

name: Franz Schubert
bio:
Schubert was born in Vienna in 1797, the son of a schoolmaster. As a boy he sang in the choir of the imperial court chapel, which came with a place at a boarding school, where he played in the student orchestra and had lessons with Antonio Salieri. For a few years he taught at his father’s school, but what he really did was write music, at an astonishing rate.

He never held an important post, and he was never famous in the way Beethoven was, though they lived in the same city. Instead he had a devoted circle of friends, who gathered for evenings of his music that came to be called Schubertiades. He wrote more than 600 songs, among them *Erlkönig*, composed when he was 18, and the song cycle *Winterreise* (“Winter Journey”).

He fell seriously ill in his mid-twenties and died in 1828, aged just 31. Much of his greatest music, including the *Unfinished* Symphony and the *Great* C major Symphony, was only performed in public years after his death. His gift was melody, but also mood: in Schubert, a sudden change of key can feel like a cloud passing over the sun.

name: Dmitri Shostakovich
bio:
Shostakovich was born in St Petersburg in 1906. After his father died, the teenager helped support the family by playing the piano in cinemas, accompanying silent films. He studied at the Petrograd Conservatory, and his First Symphony, written as a graduation piece when he was 19, made him famous almost overnight; within a few years it was being played in Berlin and in the United States.

His life was bound up with Soviet politics. In 1936 the Communist Party newspaper *Pravda* attacked his opera *Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District* as “muddle instead of music”, a dangerous charge at the height of Stalin’s purges. He answered in 1937 with his Fifth Symphony, which was greeted with a long ovation. In 1948 he was denounced again, and for years he kept some of his most personal works in a drawer.

During the Second World War his Seventh Symphony, the *Leningrad*, became a symbol of resistance; in 1942 it was even performed in the besieged city itself. He wrote fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets, music that can be savagely ironic one moment and desolate the next. People still argue about what his music was trying to say, which may be part of its power. He died in Moscow in 1975.

name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
bio:
Tchaikovsky was born in 1840 in Votkinsk, a factory town in the Urals where his father managed the ironworks. His family steered him towards a safe career: he trained in law and worked as a clerk at the Ministry of Justice in St Petersburg. In his early twenties he began to study music seriously, and he was among the first students of the new St Petersburg Conservatory.

In 1866 he moved to Moscow to teach harmony at the conservatory there. Success came gradually, with the First Piano Concerto, the ballet *Swan Lake* and the opera *Eugene Onegin*. A wealthy widow, Nadezhda von Meck, paid him an allowance for thirteen years that let him compose full time, on condition that they never meet. His brief marriage in 1877 was a disaster: Tchaikovsky was gay, at a time when that had to be hidden.

By the 1880s he was the first Russian composer whose music was celebrated internationally, and he conducted his work in Leipzig, London and New York, where he took part in the opening of Carnegie Hall in 1891. He died in St Petersburg in 1893, nine days after conducting the premiere of his Sixth Symphony, the *Pathétique*. The official cause was cholera, and it is still argued over.
